Copper-Catalyzed Enantioselective Radical Cyanation of Allenic
C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H Bonds to Access Tri- and Tetrasubstituted Chiral Allenes
Daqi Lv, Xiaotao Zhu,* and Hongli Bao*
ABSTRACT: The asymmetric radical functionalization of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H bonds represents an appealing strategy for synthesizing
axially chiral allenes. This method enables us to generate the more structurally complex and highly functionalized axially chiral
allenes directly by using the readily accessible and less substituted racemic allenes while concurrently achieving apparent dynamic
kinetic resolution. However, compared to alkyne derivative-based approaches, the asymmetric functionalization of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H
bonds remains a challenge primarily due to the intertwined demands of chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. Here, we report a
copper-catalyzed asymmetric cyanation of allenic
\mathrm { C } ( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bonds by using a substituted oxazoline chiral ligand. This strategy
eficiently transforms low-substituted racemic allenes into highly functionalized, axially chiral allenyl nitriles in a highly chemo-,
regio-, and enantioselective manner.
KEYWORDS: enantioselective cyanation, C−H functionalization, radical, chiral allene, copper catalysis
■ INTRODUCTION
Axially chiral allenes are a class of significant organic molecules,
characterized by their distinctive orthogonal twisted π-
systems.<sup>1</sup> Functionalized allenes often exhibit notable physio-
logical activities, such as enzyme inhibition, cytotoxicity, and
antibacterial properties (Scheme 1a).<sup>2</sup> As a result, structural
modifications of allene compounds or their incorporation into
pharmaceutical molecules to enhance biological activity
represent a key direction for future development in this field.<sup>3</sup>
Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in
the development of radical synthesis methods for allenes.
Among these advancements, the asymmetric transformation of
allenyl radicals has emerged as a powerful strategy for
constructing axially chiral allenes (Scheme 1b, left). Our
group previously reported the first copper-catalyzed radical 1,4-
bifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, achieving asymmetric 1,4-
oxycyanation and ofering a novel method for synthesizing
elusive axially chiral allenes.<sup>5</sup> Subsequently, Deng et al.
demonstrated a stereoselective decarboxylation strategy for
1,3-enynes using a photoinduced dual catalytic system.<sup>6</sup>
Meanwhile, Liu<sup>7</sup> and Guo<sup>8</sup> independently achieved copper-
catalyzed asymmetric 1,4-alkylalkynylation and arylalkynylation
via allenyl radical-terminal alkyne coupling. Notably, He et al.
introduced a nickel-catalyzed radical cascade reaction for
enantio- and regioselective 1,4-arylalkylation of 1,3-enynes.<sup>9</sup>
These enantioselective radical 1,4-difunctionalization protocols
collectively provide eficient access to structurally diverse,
enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes. Expanding the scope
further, Liu et al. reported copper-catalyzed enantioselective
radical cyanation of propargylic
\mathrm { C } ( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bonds, delivering
chiral trisubstituted allenyl nitriles.<sup>10</sup> These outstanding works
demonstrate that constructing axially chiral allenes from alkyne
derivatives, such as 1,3-enynes or alkynes, has become a
reliable and promising strategy.

(Scheme 1b, right). This approach enables the functionaliza-

trisubstituted allenyl nitriles. Under the standard reaction
conditions, a spectrum of enantioenriched trisubstituted allenyl
nitriles (5a−5j) was successfully synthesized. The process
demonstrates the well tolerance for diverse functional groups,

(5e), and secondary and tertiary alkyl groups (5f and 5g).
Products 5h−5j can also be obtained in good yields as well as
with higher enantioselectivities by our method.<sup>12a,13a</sup> More-
over, scaling up the reaction has led to a further enhancement
in enantioselectivity, as evidenced by product 5c, which
achieved an enantiomeric ratio of 96:4.

the allenyl radical intermediate (Scheme 4b). Kinetic isotope

\left( k _ { \mathrm { H } } / k _ { \mathrm { D } } \ = \ 2 . 3 \right)

(Scheme 4c).

We then proceeded to investigate the nonlinear efects in
this method and found that allenyl nitrile 3a indeed exhibited
linear efects (Scheme 4d).<sup>18</sup> This led us to consider that a
monoligand copper complex acts as the active catalytic species
in the reaction.<sup>19</sup> To delve deeper into the structure of the
metal complex, we conducted control experiments under
standard conditions using ligand L8, with its hydroxyl group
protected by trimethylsilyl; these results closely mirrored those
obtained under standard conditions (Scheme 4e, 58% yield,
93:7 er vs 50% yield, 93:7 er). This finding implies that the
hydroxyl group as an electron-donating group may be a
spectator and the hydrogen bonding may not play a role in the
metal complex. Furthermore, the structure of L7CuBr (16)
was elucidated through X-ray crystallography, revealing the
complex composed of a single copper atom and a single ligand
(Scheme 4f). Upon subjecting this crystal to a cyanation
reaction as the catalyst, we observed that the reaction
eficiencies and enantioselectivities were nearly identical to
those under standard conditions (47% yield, 92:8 er), thereby
validating the existence of a monoligand copper active species.
This is also consistent with the conclusions drawn from the
linear efect observed earlier.
Drawing from these experimental outcomes, we propose a
potential catalytic cycle mechanism (Scheme 5). Initially, a
monovalent monoligand copper species A undergoes single-
electron transfer with NFSI, leading to the formation of a
divalent fluorinated copper species B and a nitrogen radical.
This nitrogen radical can abstract the
\mathbf { C } ( \mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bond from
the allene, forming an allenyl radical.<sup>12a,13a</sup> The divalent
fluorinated copper species B then undergoes transmetalation
with TMSCN, yielding cyanated copper intermediate C.
Ultimately, intermediate C engages in an asymmetric func-
tional group transfer with the allenyl radical, yielding the target
product and regenerating the catalyst.
■ CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have developed a copper-catalyzed
enantioselective radical cyanation of allenic
\mathrm { C } ( \mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - H }
bonds
under mild reaction conditions, enabling eficient access to
trisubstituted and tetrasubstituted axially chiral allenyl nitriles.
This strategy achieves high chemoselectivity, regioselectivity,
and enantioselectivity, with broad functional group tolerance.
Mechanistic studies corroborate a radical pathway involving a
monoligand copper species. The synthetic utility of this
method is further highlighted by its scalability (10 mmol scale)
and the versatile downstream derivatization with a chiral
quaternary carbon center of chiral allenyl nitriles into cyclic
ether, lactam, and butenolides. We believe that this work may
open up new possibilities of allenic C(sp<sup>2</sup>)−H asymmetric
functionalization, ofering a promising entry to highly
functionalized axially chiral allene derivatives.
